about.title: About XESpresso
about.introduction: XESpresso collects the characteristics of event logs without collecting the logs themselves. It runs in your browser, so your event data never leaves your computer: it computes the FEEED features of a log, records its metadata following Costa et al. and shows where it lies among the collected logs. You can then send the features and metadata to the collection. The collection combines seven data collections: BPIC (BPI Challenge logs), Synthetic Benchmark, 4TU Real-Life Logs, Community Repositories (GitHub and Kaggle), IoPT (IoT lab logs), OCEL Publication (object-centric event logs) and SuXXES. This version lists a sample in full. The other logs are still under review: they appear as faint points, and their FEEED features are used in all analyses, without names or sources.

sections.title: Event Data Catalog
sections.summary: Browse, search and filter all event datasets with their metadata, and see them in a landscape by publication year.
sections.content: Browse, search and filter all event datasets. Metadata follows the groups of Costa et al.: Basic Process Analytics, Domain Context, Academic Context, Data Characteristics, Resource Context and Path Observation. The landscape arranges logs by Academic Context Year (of the referencing paper, else of the dataset) and colors them by the chosen concept. Filters and search apply on every page.

sections.title: Event Data Space
sections.summary: A map of the event datasets by their FEEED features: similar datasets lie close together.
sections.content: A 2D PCA of the FEEED features: each feature vector is mean-imputed, min-max scaled, L2-normalized and reduced to two components. Points are colored by Data Origin, with a hull per Data Collection; both can be set to any concept. Filtering recomputes the projection, so the axes change. Logs split from an OCEL per object type can be near-trivial and gather at one edge.

sections.title: Feature Correlations
sections.summary: How the FEEED features correlate, and which repeat each other the least.
sections.content: A heatmap of pairwise correlations between FEEED features (over the logs that have both values), grouped into eight families. A greedy selector picks the N least mutually correlated features. Filtering recomputes both when at least five logs match.

sections.title: Data Source
sections.content: One private table holds all event logs, one row each: source (DOI or dataset page), Data Collection, Dataset Source (the published dataset and its DOI), descriptive metadata (as coded by Costa et al. for their logs) and FEEED features. The public version shows a sample in full and hides the rest.

sections.title: Adding and Sending Event Data
sections.summary: Add XES, XES YAML or CSV files. Features are computed in your browser, files are never uploaded, and you can send the entries to the collection.
sections.content: Several XES files can be added separately or bundled into one log. XES YAML files (one per case, as written by CPEE, also zipped) give one log per process model. For CSV, choose the case ID, activity, timestamp and, optionally, resource columns. For an OCEL, choose one case ID column per object type to get one log per type. Logs made from one file are linked and count as one event data source. A DOI lookup fills in the year, citation, description and Dataset Source. Added logs stay in your browser. Before sending, a preview shows each entry. Send entries as a downloaded file by email or as a public GitHub issue. They contain only the computed values, your descriptions and, if given, your name and institution. The maintainers review every entry before publishing it under CC BY 4.0.
